builder_plan.scenario: You already need task-specific training and want to reduce its memory or compute cost.
builder_plan.change: Change only the training technique on a small controlled run after checking prerequisites.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current training recipe with the same model, data split, and evaluation.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Held-out quality, peak memory, training time, and full compute cost to the target quality.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: GRADS: Graph-Regulated Agentic Data Synthesis with Controllable Difficulty
summary: GRADS replaces uncontrolled seed-task expansion pipelines for synthetic agent training data with a closed loop that maintains an evidence-and-inference dependency graph, conditioning generation on relevant subgraphs and verifying that intended difficulty matches empirical difficulty. It costs a multi-stage generation-and-verification pipeline (seed selection, expansion, QA construction, verification) requiring repeated strong-LLM calls plus an independent solver for difficulty calibration, followed by SFT and RL post-training runs. It can fail if the verifier or independent solver shares biases with the generator, if the dependency graph omits implicit reasoning steps, or if gains on the authors' domain-specific benchmarks do not transfer to the reader's corpus and tool stack.
rationale: The method is implementable with third-party APIs and a single 24 GB GPU for 4B-scale post-training, but its difficulty-separation and benchmark-matching claims are validated only on the authors' domains, so workload-specific validation is required before production adoption.
technique: Graph-regulated synthetic data synthesis for agent post-training

claims.statement: GRADS replaces uncontrolled seed-task expansion pipelines for synthetic agent training data with a closed loop that maintains an evidence-and-inference dependency graph, conditioning generation on relevant subgraphs and verifying that intended difficulty matches empirical difficulty. It costs a multi-stage generation-and-verification pipeline (seed selection, expansion, QA construction, verification) requiring repeated strong-LLM calls plus an independent solver for difficulty calibration, followed by SFT and RL post-training runs. It can fail if the verifier or independent solver shares biases with the generator, if the dependency graph omits implicit reasoning steps, or if gains on the authors' domain-specific benchmarks do not transfer to the reader's corpus and tool stack.

SFT on GRADS data raises solution-termination rate above 95% while cutting tool calls and turns by up to 75%; RL trims tool use by up to a further 19.5%, and the resulting 4B model matches Sonnet 4 on software engineering and surpasses it on scientific and security held-out benchmarks.
